summary: Describes security threats to the Reliable Server Pooling architecture and sets out requirements for security to counter them. RSerPool manages and provides access to pools of servers for highly reliable applications. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5355 lists the ways the RSerPool protocols can be attacked and the requirement that answers each one. Most of the answers involve TLS, used with a shared secret for registration and with certificates for looking up a server.

subtitle: What can go wrong when a protocol stands between a client and its server, and how each case is answered.

tldr.problem: RSerPool inserts a session layer between a client and a server, so that a session can be moved to a different server. That breaks the usual assumption that the two ends of a connection know who they are talking to.
tldr.mechanism: The document lists seventeen threats against the architecture, gives the effect of each, and states the requirement that answers it, then summarises the mechanisms required for each component of the protocol suite.
tldr.outcome: TLS was selected as the security mechanism for the suite, with pre-shared keys mandatory for registration and certificates mandatory for handle resolution. Insider attacks by a rogue but authenticated server remain unsolved.

today: RFC 5355 is an Informational document and is not listed as obsoleted or updated. It is the threat analysis for RSerPool. The mechanisms it requires are described in the Security Considerations sections of RFC 5352 and RFC 5353.

sections.title: Introduction: What a Session Layer Changes
sections.content:
RSerPool supports high availability and load balancing by letting a pool user identify the most appropriate server in a pool at a given time. Its goals are application-independent protocol mechanisms, separation of server naming from IP addressing, the end-to-end principle, separation of session availability and failover functionality from the application, support for different server selection policies, a set of application-independent failover capabilities, and a peer-to-peer structure.

RSerPool provides a session layer for robustness, and that layer may redirect communication transparently to the layers above. This alters the direct one-to-one association between communicating endpoints that normally exists between clients and servers. Secure operation of protocols often relies on assumptions at different layers about the identity of the communicating party and about the continuity of the communication between endpoints. The operation of RSerPool itself also has security implications, and because the session layer operates dynamically, it imposes further concerns for the end-to-end security of the application. The document explores the security implications of RSerPool both from its own functions and from being interposed between applications and transport interfaces.

The document is related to the Aggregate Server Access Protocol, RFC 5352, and the Endpoint Name Resolution Protocol, RFC 5353, whose Security Considerations sections describe the mechanisms for meeting the requirements set out here. TLS, RFC 5246, was selected as the security mechanism for RSerPool because it meets all the requirements described.

The terms used are the operational scope, which is the part of the network visible to pool users by a specific instance of the Reliable Server Pooling protocols; the pool, a collection of servers providing the same application functionality; the pool handle, a logical pointer to a pool that is unique within the operational scope; the ENRP handlespace, a cohesive structure of pool names and relations that may be queried by a client; the pool element, a server entity that has registered to a pool; and the pool user.
sections.plainLanguage: The trouble with RSerPool is that it sits between the client and the server and can move the session elsewhere. Security normally depends on both ends knowing who the other is, and on the link staying the same link. Both assumptions are weakened here, so the document works through what has to be protected.

sections.title: Attacks on Registration and on the ENRP Server Group
sections.content:
Five threats share a shape: a party that should not be able to write to the registry does so, and the registry believes it.

  • A malicious node can send a stream of false registrations and de-registrations on behalf of pool elements that do not exist, at a very rapid rate, creating unnecessary state in an ENRP server. The effect is a corrupted pool registrar database or a disabled discovery function, which is a denial of service because a pool user could get the address of a non-existent element in response to a query. The requirement is that an ENRP server MUST NOT create or update state until it has authenticated the element, with TLS using a pre-shared key mandatory to implement. For a pre-shared key, having the key constitutes authorization, so the network administrators of a pool decide which nodes may take part. The justification is the assumption that one administrative domain controls and manages the server pool, which lets the key be managed by a central security administrator.
  • A malicious node or element can send registrations that it is not authorized to send, at a very rapid rate. The effects are denial of service, where a user gets the address of a rogue element and a flood of messages prevents legitimate elements from registering, and data interception, where the rogue element provides the service as a man in the middle and collects the data. Again the ENRP server MUST NOT create or update state until the authentication information of the registering entity is verified.
  • A malicious node can send false registrations about a legitimate element, creating false state that is propagated to the other ENRP servers and corrupting the database. A distributed denial of service can follow, because an attacker registers an address for a popular service and the users connect to it instead, allowing man-in-the-middle or masquerade attacks and eavesdropping on the service data. The requirement is the same authentication rule, plus that a pool element can register only for itself and never on behalf of other elements.
  • A pool element that is not authorized to join a pool can send registrations and de-registrations directly, with the same effect of false state propagated across the ENRP servers and the same opening for man-in-the-middle and masquerade attacks. The requirement here is that the ENRP server MUST NOT create or update state until it has authorized the requesting entity.
  • A malicious node can set up an ENRP server of its own and try to join the group of legitimate ones, to propagate inaccurate updates. The effect is an inconsistent ENRP database state. The requirement is that ENRP servers MUST perform mutual authentication, with TLS as the mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: Most of these attacks work the same way: something sends the registry a registration it should not be allowed to send, and the registry stores it. The rule that answers them is that the registry must check who is talking before it writes anything down, and that the check must work in both directions so that a fake registry cannot join the group either.

sections.title: Attacks on Resolution, Failover, Integrity and Confidentiality
sections.content:
A pool element that unknowingly registers with a malicious ENRP server may have its registration ignored or not processed properly, and a rogue ENRP server can return any address it likes to a user asking for service, which can cause denial of service or a connection to an element of the attacker's choosing. The requirement is that the pool element MUST authenticate the ENRP server, with TLS using a pre-shared key mandatory, and this also prevents malicious insiders and outsiders from adding their own ENRP server to the pool.

Related to that, ASAP can receive a handlespace resolution response from a malicious ENRP server that returns random IP addresses or an inaccurate list for a pool handle. The pool user then talks to the wrong element, or cannot find the element at all, and a rogue server can steer the user to an element of its choice where the attacker can eavesdrop or tamper with the application. The requirement is that ASAP SHOULD authenticate the ENRP server, and here TLS with certificates is the mandatory mechanism: a centralized certificate authority generates and signs the certificate, the certificate is stored on the ENRP server, the trusted root certificate is sent to the client out of band, and the signature on the server certificate is checked during the TLS handshake.

A malicious node can replay an entire message previously sent by a legitimate entity, creating false state, most likely as a denial of service if the replay de-registers every pool element. The requirement is that the protocol MUST prevent replay attacks, and the replay protection in TLS meets it.

Failover creates its own problem. When a pool user fails over from element A to element B, a trust relationship it had with A will not exist with B, which violates security policy: if the security context with A involved encryption and the one with B does not, an attacker can exploit the change. The requirement is that the application SHOULD be notified when failover occurs so it can establish a trusted relationship with B, and ENRP has a mechanism for this.

Three threats are instances of the same class: the ENRP response to a pool handle resolution is corrupted in transit, ENRP peer messages are corrupted, or an element's update is corrupted. The result is that ASAP receives corrupt information which the pool user believes to be accurate, possibly an IP address that does not resolve to an element, so the user cannot reach the server. The requirement is that an integrity mechanism MUST be present on the interfaces from a pool element to an ENRP server and from an ENRP server to an ENRP server, and TLS provides it.

For confidentiality, an eavesdropper snooping on fields within messages in transit may gather information such as topology, location and IP addresses that the administrator does not want to divulge, and use it for financial gain or for attacks on hosts. A provision for data confidentiality SHOULD be available, and TLS provides it.

Server discovery has its own threats. An attacker can thwart discovery, by reducing the set of ENRP servers a pool element hears about to nothing or to a small set of inactive ones, which makes the element believe that no ENRP server is available and keeps it out of the pool. The same applies when an ENRP server or ASAP on behalf of a pool user needs to discover servers. An attacker can also spoof discovery by claiming to be a legitimate ENRP server, which it can only do if no security mechanisms are used, and a spoofed server can misrepresent, ignore, hide or distort information about a pool element. The requirement is that a provision for authentication MUST be present and a provision for data confidentiality SHOULD be present.
sections.plainLanguage: The next set of attacks target the lookup and the failover. A fake registry can answer with whatever address it likes, an old message can be sent again to undo registrations, and a corrupted reply can send a client to an address that does not work. Failover has its own subtlety: the client trusted the old server and does not trust the new one, so it must be told.

sections.title: Insider Attacks and the Limits of TLS
sections.content:
The document does not cover every byzantine attack that could come from legitimate ENRP servers. True protection against misbehavior by authentic but rogue servers is beyond the capability of TLS, because authentication using TLS does not protect against byzantine attacks: an authenticated ENRP server might itself have been maliciously hacked. Protections against insider attacks are generally specific to the attack, so more experimentation is needed. Two examples are given.

The first is that legitimate users may choose not to follow the proposed policies about which servers to use. If the policy is to choose a member at random, a pool user can always set its random choices so that it picks a particular pool member, which bypasses the load sharing behind the policy. The second is that a pool member may report a wrong policy to a user. To mitigate the first, the protocol may require the pool user to prove that the member was chosen randomly, for example by demonstrating that the choice was the result of applying a hash function to a public nonce; other methods may suit other member scheduling policies. To mitigate the second, the protocol might require the pool element to sign the policy it sends to the ENRP server, and to send that signed policy from the ENRP server to an ASAP endpoint in a way that lets the user hold the server accountable to the policy later.
sections.plainLanguage: Some attacks come from inside, from a registry server that is properly authenticated but has been taken over. TLS cannot help with that, because it only proves who a server is. The document offers two ideas for the specific cases it describes: proving that a server was picked at random, and signing the policy a server reports so a user can check it later.

sections.title: The Required Security Mechanisms, by Component
sections.content:
The document summarises the security service required for each architectural component, noting which mechanisms are required and which are optional. The first four threats, combined with the sixth, result in a requirement for mutual authentication between the ENRP server and the pool element. In summary, the first twelve threats require mechanisms that support authentication, integrity, data confidentiality and protection from replay attacks, and RSerPool needs to authenticate three relationships: the pool user authenticates the ENRP server, the pool element and the ENRP server authenticate each other, and ENRP servers authenticate each other.

For the RSerPool client, mandatory-to-implement authentication of the ENRP server is required for accurate pool handle resolution, to protect against rogue ENRP servers, and confidentiality, integrity and replay protection are also mandatory to implement, to protect against eavesdropping and against data corruption or false data transmission. For pool element to ENRP communications, mandatory-to-implement mutual authentication, integrity and replay protection are required, to protect the integrity of the ENRP handlespace database, and confidentiality is mandatory to implement and is used when privacy is required. The same set is required for ENRP to ENRP communications.

Two further requirements limit message floods. The number of endpoint-unreachable messages sent to the ENRP server by the pool user SHOULD be limited, a mechanism described in the ASAP document, because a flood of them is a denial of service on the ENRP server, which could not service other users or take registrations in a timely manner, nor update the other ENRP servers in the pool promptly. ENRP MUST limit the frequency of Keep-Alive messages to a given pool element, to prevent the element from being overwhelmed and unable to service its clients.

Two requirements concern the ENRP database and the cookie mechanism. Either the entire ENRP server database MUST be secure, meaning it has registrations exclusively from elements that used security mechanisms, or the entire database MUST be insecure, meaning registrations come from elements that used none. ENRP servers that support security MUST reject any registration that does not use the security mechanisms, and MUST NOT accept updates from other ENRP servers that do not use them, so any information not sent using TLS to a secure ENRP server MUST be rejected. On cookies, the application layer is out of scope for RSerPool, but cookies travel over the ASAP control channel, and where TCP is the transport the data and control channels must be multiplexed, so a case where the control channel is secured and the data channel is not is not possible. If the element signs or encrypts the cookie it must share keys with the other elements, and that application-level state sharing is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The summary is a checklist. Every client must check the registry before trusting its answer, every registry must check every element before storing what it says, and registries must check each other. Integrity, confidentiality and replay protection are required on all three links. Two message floods are rate-limited, the database must be either wholly secured or wholly unsecured, and the state cookie travels inside the protected control channel.

viz.caption: THE THREE RELATIONSHIPS THAT MUST BE AUTHENTICATED

items.title: Pool user to ENRP server
items.text: The pool user authenticates the ENRP server, so that it can trust the address it gets back.

items.title: Pool element to ENRP server
items.text: Mutual authentication, so that neither side can be fooled about who the other is.

items.title: ENRP server to ENRP server
items.text: Mutual authentication, so that a rogue registry cannot join the group and spread false entries.
